Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 00371| 00372| #### Respecting reduced motion 00373| 00374| Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 00375| 00376| The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 00377| 00378| ```css filename="app/globals.css" 00379| @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 00380| ::view-transition-old(*), 00381| ::view-transition-new(*), 00382| ::view-transition-group(*) { 00383| animation-duration: 0s !important; 00384| animation-delay: 0s !important; 00385| } 00386| } 00387| ``` 00388| 00389| Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 00390| 00391| ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 00392| 00393| The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 00394| 00395| A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 00396| 00397| Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 00398| 00399| ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 00400| import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 00401| 00402| export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 00403| const { slug } = await params 00404| 00405| return ( 00406| }> 00407| 00414| 00415| 00416| 00417| ) 00418| } 00419| ``` 00420| 00421| The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 00422| 00423| If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 00424| 00425| ## Next steps 00426| 00427| You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location. 00428| 00429| Each pattern answers a different question for the user: 00430| 00431| | Pattern | What it communicates | 00432| | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | 00433| | Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper" | 00434| | Suspense reveal | "Data loaded" | 00435| | Directional slide | "Going forward / coming back" | 00436| | Same-route crossfade | "Same place, different content" | 00437| 00438| For API details and more patterns: 00439| 00440| - [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes) 00441| - [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router), which also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()` 00442| - [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) 00443| - [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file 00444| (End of file - total 444 lines)

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

## React Compiler Support

Built-in support for the React Compiler is now stable in **Next.js 16** following the React Compiler's 1.0 release. The React Compiler automatically memoizes components, reducing unnecessary re-renders with zero manual code changes.

The `reactCompiler` configuration option has been promoted from `experimental` to stable. It is not enabled by default as we continue gathering build performance data across different application types.
